title: The Memo Congress Never Voted On
hook: A presidential memorandum can direct 200-plus FBI task forces to hunt down a whole ideology — no bill, no vote, and no requirement it even be made public.
key_points: A national security presidential memorandum is a unilateral executive directive — unlike a law, it needs no congressional vote and, unlike most executive orders, isn't required to be published.

NSPM-7, issued in September 2025, directs the FBI's 200-plus Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate 'radicalizing' people toward political violence and lets the Attorney General designate groups as domestic terrorist organizations.
It authorizes preemptive disruption of groups before any violent act, using ideological markers like 'anti-Christian' or 'anti-capitalism' views as indicators, per legal analysis in The Conversation.
Congress has never passed a domestic-terrorism designation law, partly out of concern that labeling groups by ideology risks punishing First Amendment-protected speech and association.

Thirty-one members of Congress formally objected in October 2025, warning the memo poses serious constitutional, statutory, and civil-liberties risks — objections with no binding force, since the memo itself never needed their approval.
content_html: Some of the most consequential national-security decisions never touch a congressional vote. A presidential memorandum is a tool the executive branch can use entirely on its own — and one law professor's analysis argues the Trump administration's latest domestic-terrorism campaign is built on exactly that kind of unchecked authority.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, Melinda Haas details National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), issued in September 2025, which directs the FBI's more than 200 Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate people "radicalizing" toward political violence and empowers the Attorney General to designate groups as domestic terrorist organizations — including preemptive disruption before any violent act occurs, using ideological markers like "anti-Christian" or "anti-capitalism" views as indicators. Congress has deliberately never passed its own domestic-terrorism designation statute, largely over concern that targeting groups by ideology risks punishing speech and association the First Amendment protects. NSPM-7 sidesteps that debate entirely: as a memorandum rather than legislation, it required no vote and isn't even guaranteed to be public. Thirty-one members of Congress formally objected in October 2025, calling it a serious constitutional and civil-liberties risk — an objection that, tellingly, carries no binding force, since the memo never needed their approval to take effect in the first place. (This card describes U.S. federal executive practice specifically.)

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Melinda Haas, Assistant Professor of International Affairs, University of Pittsburgh

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: The Executive
related.hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

related.title: Freedom of Expression
related.hook: The freedom to speak, publish, and dissent is often called the first freedom — because without it, citizens can't check power or argue their way to better decisions.

related.title: Terrorism
related.hook: Terrorism is violence aimed less at its victims than at an audience — using fear as a political weapon to force change a group cannot win by other means.

flashcards.prompt: How is a national security presidential memorandum different from a law Congress passes?
flashcards.back_html: It's a unilateral executive directive — no congressional vote is needed, and unlike most executive orders, it isn't even required to be published or made public.

flashcards.prompt: What does NSPM-7, issued in September 2025, direct federal task forces to do?

choices.text: Investigate people 'radicalizing' toward political violence and allow the AG to designate groups as domestic terrorist organizations
Create a new federal domestic-terrorism statute that must be approved by Congress
Transfer terrorism investigations entirely from the FBI to state police

flashcards.explanation_html: Per The Conversation's analysis, NSPM-7 directs 200-plus Joint Terrorism Task Forces toward this mission — entirely through presidential directive, not legislation.

flashcards.prompt: Why has Congress never passed its own domestic-terrorism designation law, according to the analysis?

choices.text: Concern that labeling groups by ideology risks punishing First Amendment-protected speech and association
The Supreme Court had already ruled such a law unconstitutional
No lawmaker had ever proposed one before 2025

flashcards.explanation_html: That First Amendment concern is exactly what critics say the memo sidesteps by acting through presidential directive instead of statute.
